items.title: The Windrush passengers were British subjects, not foreign immigrants
items.claim: On 22 June 1948 the HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury with 492 passengers from the Caribbean. Their legal status?

options.text: They required visas and work permits
They were British subjects with full right of entry — the British Nationality Act 1948 confirmed Commonwealth citizens' status, passed weeks after Windrush
They were refugees with temporary leave
They were on military service tickets only

items.reveal:
The British Nationality Act 1948 (royal assent 30 July 1948) defined 'Citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies' alongside Commonwealth citizenship. Caribbean people were British subjects; the journey required no permit.

The 1971 Immigration Act removed automatic right of abode for most Commonwealth citizens. People who had arrived as children before 1973 should have had right to remain, but the Home Office destroyed landing card records in 2010 — leading to the Windrush scandal of 2018, when long-resident citizens were detained, deported or denied healthcare.

The Windrush brought around 1,000 passengers total, including Jamaicans returning from RAF service.
items.why: Right of abode in Britain has been redefined repeatedly. The 1948-1973 period when Commonwealth citizens had unrestricted entry is bracketed by very different regimes — and the 2018 scandal shows what happens when administrative memory fails.

items.title: The Korean War killed around 3 million people
items.claim: What was the death toll of the Korean War (June 1950-July 1953)?

options.text: Estimates centre around 3 million dead, mostly Korean civilians; nearly 37,000 US, around 1,000 British and Commonwealth, and over 400,000 Chinese troops killed
Comparable to WWI losses for the Allies

items.reveal:
North Korea invaded south of the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950. UN forces under General MacArthur landed at Inchon (September 1950) and pushed to the Yalu River; China entered in October-November.

The armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953. There has never been a peace treaty — the two Koreas are still technically at war. Pyongyang was reduced by US bombing to perhaps 25% of its buildings; an estimated 20% of North Korea's population died.

In the US, sandwiched between WWII and Vietnam, it became 'the forgotten war' despite high casualties.
items.why: Conflict casualties are not just about combatant deaths. Korea's civilian toll, the bombing intensity and the legacy of an unresolved war shape East Asia today — but rarely feature in Cold War textbooks.

items.title: WWI was triggered by a wrong turn
items.claim: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand survived the first assassination attempt that morning. What caused the second, successful attempt hours later?

options.text: A coordinated second wave of assassins ambushed his motorcade on the way to the hospital
His driver took a wrong turn into a side street, stalled the car, and stopped directly in front of Gavrilo Princip
Princip followed the motorcade by tram and intercepted it at the town hall
A Serbian double agent inside the security detail signalled his location

items.reveal_title: A wrong turn into world war
items.reveal:
After a bomb attack that morning failed, the Archduke insisted on visiting the wounded at the hospital. His driver, Leopold Lojka, had not been told the route had been changed. He turned right onto Franz Joseph Street, was told he was going the wrong way, and stalled while reversing.

Gavrilo Princip, who had given up and was eating a sandwich (the sandwich story is disputed but he was at Schiller's delicatessen), happened to be standing there. He stepped forward and fired twice from five feet away.
items.why: The 'causes of WWI' essay tends to load every variable onto structural forces (alliances, militarism, imperialism). Those forces created the powder keg, but a stalled car lit the fuse. Contingency matters.
